title: Unapproved BITS Job Notification Commands
exclusions: Detects Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational event 6 records that contain a nonempty BITS notification program and lack an exact, in-window approval for normalized host, job owner, and full program-plus-parameters hash. It detects configuration of a command-line callback, not job creation, file addition, transfer start/completion, callback execution, persistence success, payload content, malicious intent, or compromise. Microsoft documents that SetNotifyCmdLine can request execution when a job enters ERROR or TRANSFERRED state, but service-account jobs do not execute command-line callbacks and a valid COM callback can prevent command execution; this rule must not claim every event 6 launches a process. It does not cover BITS jobs without notification commands, event providers/versions whose event 6 template differs, PowerShell/BITSAdmin command attempts that never set the property, transfer URLs, BITS database forensics, direct COM telemetry, process/network behavior, or non-Windows transfer systems. This documentation review did not validate the provider template, collection, lookup, SPL, or alert in production.
evidence: Retain covered-host/OS inventory; BITS Client Operational channel and provider metadata exports (`wevtutil gp Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client /ge:true` or equivalent); raw event 6 XML; BITS policy and current-job inventories where authorized; `windows_bits_notify_command_approvals.csv` revision and approvals; saved search `windows_unapproved_bits_notify_commands` definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; source/schema-health reports; process/PowerShell/EDR correlation; alert actions; incident dispositions; and dated positive, approved, expired, wrong-hash, blank-program, version-drift, duplicate-route, service-owner, and callback-execution/nonexecution tests. Preserve host, event/index time, provider/channel/version, record ID, job ID/owner, raw and normalized program/parameters, command hash, approval state/revision, raw event identity, and analyst conclusion. Documentation review generated no runtime evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index, ingest one XML event from provider `Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client`, channel `Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational`, EventCode 6, with `Computer=bits-lab-01`, `EventRecordID=6001`, `jobId={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`, `jobOwner=LAB\\analyst`, `program=C:\\Windows\\System32\\wscript.exe`, and `parameters=C:\\Windows\\System32\\wscript.exe C:\\Users\\Public\\job.vbs`; provide no matching approval. Expect exactly one row with normalized host/owner/program, a deterministic SHA-256 command hash, and `approval_state=unapproved`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: For the same event, publish an exact lookup row keyed by `bits-lab-01`, normalized `lab\\analyst`, and the SHA-256 of normalized program plus `|` plus normalized parameters; set inclusive start at or before event time and exclusive end after it, with nonempty approval ID, owner, approver, and revision. Expect zero alert rows while retaining the approved base event separately. Also expect zero rows for event 3 job creation, event 16403 file addition, event 6 with empty program, wrong provider/channel, missing job ID/owner/record ID, and a duplicate of EventRecordID 6001. Expired, future, wrong-host, wrong-owner, or one-character-different command hash approvals must still yield one row.

dataSources: Primary source: provider `Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client`, channel `Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational`, event 6, collected in XML or classic rendering with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742). On every supported Windows build, export provider metadata and raw XML to prove that event 6 represents a command-line command set for a BITS job and that its local template exposes `jobId`, `jobOwner`, `program`, and `parameters`; also retain host/computer, provider, channel, event version, EventRecordID/RecordNumber, event time, and index time. Microsoft does not publish a stable per-event web schema for this provider, so local manifest/template verification is mandatory. Governance source: exact time-bounded approval rows keyed by normalized host, job owner, and SHA-256 of normalized program plus parameters.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for BITS Client Operational event collection and extraction. A deployment-owned endpoint security app must provide provider-template/source health, exact command approvals, saved search, fixtures, dashboard, BITS inventory correlation, and response runbook.
spl:
index=windows source IN ("WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational","XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational") sourcetype IN ("WinEventLog","XmlWinEventLog") EventCode=6 earliest=-15m@m latest=@m
| eval sample_host=lower(coalesce(Computer,dest,host)), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber), provider=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName), job_id=lower(coalesce(jobId,JobId)), job_owner=lower(trim(coalesce(jobOwner,JobOwner))), program_raw=program, parameters_raw=parameters, notify_program=lower(trim(program)), notify_parameters=lower(replace(trim(coalesce(parameters,"")),"\\s+"," "))
| where provider="Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client" AND len(sample_host)>0 AND len(event_record_id)>0 AND len(job_id)>0 AND len(job_owner)>0 AND len(notify_program)>0
| dedup sample_host source event_record_id
| eval command_sha256=sha256(notify_program."|".notify_parameters)
| lookup windows_bits_notify_command_approvals.csv sample_host job_owner command_sha256 OUTPUTNEW approved_start_epoch approved_end_epoch approval_id approval_owner approver approval_revision
| eval approval_complete=if(len(approval_id)>0 AND len(approval_owner)>0 AND len(approver)>0 AND len(approval_revision)>0 AND isnotnull(tonumber(approved_start_epoch)) AND isnotnull(tonumber(approved_end_epoch)),1,0), approval_state=if(approval_complete=1 AND _time>=tonumber(approved_start_epoch) AND _time<tonumber(approved_end_epoch),"approved","unapproved")
| where approval_state="unapproved"
| table _time _indextime sample_host EventCode EventRecordID event_record_id provider source sourcetype job_id job_owner program_raw parameters_raw notify_program notify_parameters command_sha256 approval_state approval_id approval_owner approver approval_revision
| sort 0 - _time sample_host event_record_id
description: Returns one event-grain row for each complete, deduplicated BITS Client Operational event 6 that configures a nonempty job notification program and has no exact valid approval for normalized host, job owner, and full normalized command hash at event time. The row proves notification-command configuration, not that BITS executed the command.
value: BITS notification commands can launch user-context code when a transfer reaches a configured state and can outlive the process that created the job. Reconciling every configured callback with narrowly approved software behavior helps defenders find unauthorized execution/persistence mechanisms while retaining enough job and command identity to investigate safely.
implementation: Enable and collect the BITS Client Operational channel, export the local Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client provider template on every supported build, and prove event 6 fields in both selected renderings. Publish an exact, normalized, hash-bound, time-limited approval lookup and separate source/schema-health searches. Save the SPL as `windows_unapproved_bits_notify_commands`, run every five minutes over a measured 15-minute arrival window, and investigate each unapproved configuration with current BITS inventory and process/script/endpoint evidence. Never equate configuration with callback execution.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — BITS Notification Command Governance`: show covered hosts missing channel telemetry or expected event-6 schema first; then unapproved commands by normalized program, owner, host, command hash, and time, plus approval-match rate, provider-version drift, duplicate routes, and disposition. Drill down to raw event 6 XML, exact approval/revision, current BITS job state and notification properties, job creation/file/transfer events, creator and callback process telemetry, PowerShell/BITSAdmin activity, network/file evidence, and ticket. Label the state “notification command configured,” never “callback executed” without process evidence.
schema: Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client Operational event 6 locally verified provider template plus exact command approval governance
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary detector. Generic Change or Endpoint.Processes acceleration does not preserve BITS job ID/owner, event-6 program and parameters, provider-template version, record identity, or exact approval interval. Process `tstats` can corroborate a later launch but cannot prove SetNotifyCmdLine configuration; a secondary normalized change may be produced only after raw-event parity is tested.

knownFalsePositives:
Event 6 is a high-value configuration record, but legitimate Windows and application software can use BITS notification programs.

1. **Microsoft or third-party updater callback** — A signed updater may register a helper to finalize installation after transfer. Verify product/version, package/deployment job, exact program and parameters, signer/hash, owner, BITS job inventory, expected transfer endpoints/files, vendor design, and bounded approval. A Microsoft-looking path or signature alone is insufficient.

2. **Enterprise software distribution** — Configuration Manager, endpoint management, package delivery, or line-of-business deployment software may use callbacks. Confirm management-agent process, assignment/package ID, host ring, service owner, exact command hash, job owner, and expected completion behavior.

3. **Security product content update or remediation** — EDR, antimalware, vulnerability, or compliance agents can use BITS and a post-transfer processor. Validate installed sensor/version, signed callback binary, policy/job ID, vendor documentation, endpoint event, and exact approved command.

4. **Developer or integration testing** — A team may exercise `IBackgroundCopyJob2::SetNotifyCmdLine`, BITSAdmin, or a custom COM client. Require named lab hosts/users, test plan, exact command hash, start/exclusive expiry, owner/approver, expected process event, and cleanup/cancel/complete evidence.

5. **Authorized red-team or purple-team exercise** — Operators may deliberately demonstrate T1197. Require exercise ID, isolated scope, named operator, exact job owner/command/hash, fixed window, expected transfer/process/network artifacts, and post-test queue cleanup.

6. **Legacy maintenance agent** — An older application may have a stable but poorly documented callback. Do not suppress on age or install path. Establish binary signature/hash, software owner, support status, exact arguments, job behavior, destination, update cadence, and replacement risk.

7. **Command normalization or lookup drift** — Case, repeated whitespace, quotes, path aliases, owner formatting, stale search-head bundle, or UTC conversion can cause an approval miss. Compare raw and normalized values, recompute SHA-256 with the documented delimiter, verify lookup revision/checksum and epochs, then correct governance.

8. **Duplicate WEC/local forwarding or replay** — The same event record can arrive through multiple routes or after queue recovery. The SPL deduplicates host/source/record ID within one dispatch; verify provider/channel record identity, source routes, index times, collector subscription, and durable checkpoint before treating repeats as new configurations.

9. **Service-account-owned job** — Microsoft states command-line callbacks do not execute for jobs in NetworkService, LocalSystem, or LocalService context. The configuration can still be unexpected and should be reviewed, but response must distinguish configured from executable. Validate owner SID/account and actual process evidence; do not blanket-suppress all service owners.

10. **Valid COM callback takes precedence** — Microsoft states BITS may not execute the command line when a registered COM callback remains valid and succeeds. This affects impact, not event legitimacy. Verify job notification interface/flags and process outcome; do not suppress configuration solely because one test did not launch.

**Safe suppression:** populate `windows_bits_notify_command_approvals.csv` before deployment with exact lowercase `sample_host`, normalized `job_owner`, SHA-256 `command_sha256` computed from `notify_program + "|" + notify_parameters`, inclusive `approved_start_epoch`, exclusive `approved_end_epoch`, `approval_id`, `approval_owner`, `approver`, and immutable `approval_revision`. Reject wildcard hosts/owners, program-only approvals, path-prefix or publisher-wide exceptions, omitted arguments, open-ended windows, retroactive entries, and missing ownership. Preserve approved base events in a restricted report. Never suppress provider/schema/source health, blank-field anomalies, job inventory drift, or duplicate-route findings.
detectionType: TTP-oriented governed BITS notification-command configuration event
hardware: Supported Windows clients and servers where Background Intelligent Transfer Service is present, the BITS Client Operational channel is available, and the installed Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client provider template has been verified to expose event 6 job/command fields. Provider versions that differ from the tested schema require separate qualification before coverage.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft BITS lifecycle, SetNotifyCmdLine, callback-execution, BITSAdmin, Windows provider-metadata, and Get-WinEvent template documentation; current MITRE ATT&CK BITS Jobs semantics; and Splunk Microsoft Windows add-on documentation; the local event-6 template, fields, lookup, SPL, fixtures, callback outcome, alerting, dashboard, and response were specified but not executed or Windows/BITS/Splunk-SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: The detector scans one normally low-volume BITS Operational event ID over 15 minutes, normalizes short strings, computes SHA-256, deduplicates record identity, and performs one exact lookup. Cost scales with covered hosts, duplicate routing, and updater activity; keep provider/channel/event restrictions in the base term.
sources: local provider metadata and schema inventory
exact BITS notification command approval lookup
optional BITS job, process, PowerShell, EDR, file, and network evidence

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and claim boundary

Assign Windows endpoint, software distribution, security operations, Splunk data/content, change governance, privacy, and incident owners. Inventory stable host identity, supported OS/build, installed BITS provider version, channel state/size/retention, BITS policies, approved software using callbacks, forwarder/WEC routes, add-on version, index/RBAC, lookup owner, and retirement time.

Understand the behavior before monitoring it. Microsoft documents BITS as an asynchronous HTTP/HTTPS/SMB transfer service whose jobs can continue after the creating application exits. `IBackgroundCopyJob2::SetNotifyCmdLine` configures a full-path program and arguments for ERROR or TRANSFERRED notifications, and BITS uses CreateProcessAsUser in the calling user's context. Microsoft also documents important limits: service-account-context jobs do not execute command-line callbacks; a valid successful COM notification interface can take precedence; and setting the property after the state event can still cause execution. Therefore event 6 is a configuration indicator, not process-execution proof.

The detector intentionally narrows the old “transfer abuse” claim. It does not inspect URLs or assert a completed download. It reports nonempty callback commands not represented by exact approval. MITRE T1197 applies because callback execution and long-lived jobs are explicitly part of BITS abuse, but the same supported API is used legitimately.

## Step 1 — Qualify the provider and channel

Microsoft does not publish a stable event-6 payload page comparable to Security audit events. Treat the installed instrumentation manifest as the event contract. On every supported Windows release/build, run elevated `wevtutil gp Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client /ge:true /gm:true /f:xml` and archive the output/checksum, or inspect `(Get-WinEvent -ListProvider Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client).Events` and each event's Template. Microsoft documents both provider metadata mechanisms.

Confirm that event ID 6 is in `Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational`, its message means a command-line command was set for a BITS job, and its template names/types are `jobId`, `jobOwner`, `program`, and `parameters`. Record event version and provider GUID. If a build lacks event 6, renames fields, or changes semantics, mark it uncovered until extraction and fixtures are revised; do not parse localized Message text as a silent fallback.

Enable and size the Operational channel through governed configuration. Preserve enough capacity for updater/install bursts and forwarding delay. Build `windows_bits_provider_schema_health` comparing host/build/provider version/template checksum and `windows_bits_operational_source_health` comparing covered inventory with recent channel ingestion, record continuity, field completeness, WEC subscriptions, and expected lab/control telemetry. No event does not mean no callback was configured.

## Step 2 — Collect and verify event rendering

Use Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742). In controlled `inputs.conf` or WEC, collect the exact BITS Client Operational channel to deployment-local `index=windows`; this is a local convention, not a product default. Test `source=WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational,sourcetype=WinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational,sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, then narrow production to actual qualified forms.

In an isolated lab, create a benign suspended BITS job, set a harmless callback to a signed test program that only writes a non-sensitive marker, and export event 6 before resuming only if callback execution testing is separately approved. Verify Computer/dest/host, provider, channel, version, EventRecordID or RecordNumber, jobId GUID, jobOwner, program, parameters, event time, and index time in raw XML and Splunk. Confirm capitalization and that program/parameters are not truncated by channel, forwarder, line breaking, or extraction.

Also remove the notification by setting both values NULL and observe the local event behavior. The primary SPL excludes empty programs because removal does not configure an executable callback; retain removal events in a separate audit report if governance requires. Verify events 3, 4, 6, 59, and 16403 are distinct on your build rather than reusing unverified internet ID labels.

## Step 3 — Govern exact command approvals

Publish `windows_bits_notify_command_approvals.csv` from software/change governance. Before hashing, lowercase and trim program, lowercase parameters, trim their ends, and collapse repeated whitespace to one space. Compute SHA-256 over `notify_program + "|" + notify_parameters`. Store exact lowercase host and job owner, command hash, inclusive start epoch, exclusive end epoch, approval ID, accountable owner, approver, immutable revision, package/product/version, expected signer/file hash, and reason.

Require one row per host/owner/command/window. Validate numeric times, start < end, bounded duration, no wildcards, no path-prefix or publisher-only rules, complete arguments, approval created before deployment, unique keys, owner existence, and lookup checksum/signature. Quoting differences can change meaning and hash; test command generation exactly as the product emits it. A broad approval for `powershell.exe`, `cmd.exe`, `wscript.exe`, or an updater directory would hide changed arguments and is forbidden.

Maintain an approved software profile outside the lookup containing expected creator, job title/purpose, transfer endpoints, local files, callback binary signer/hash, deployment ring, and lifecycle. Approval controls alert delivery; it does not prove the binary or transfer is safe at runtime.

## Step 4 — Create and understand the SPL

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_unapproved_bits_notify_commands`. Schedule every five minutes with `earliest=-15m@m latest=@m` only after measuring p99 WEC/forwarder/index delay. Use overlap plus a durable checkpoint keyed by sample_host, source, event_record_id, command_sha256, and event time so late data is caught without repeat paging.

The base search fixes local index, qualified Operational sources/renderings, and event 6. The first eval normalizes host and field-name aliases, preserves raw command strings, and normalizes job ID/owner/program/parameters. The where clause requires exact provider, complete event/job identity, and nonempty program. This rejects malformed or notification-removal records from alerting; health/audit searches retain them.

`dedup sample_host source event_record_id` handles repeats inside one route/dispatch. The detector computes SHA-256 over normalized full command, joins exact host/owner/hash approval, validates complete governance metadata and numeric times, applies inclusive start/exclusive end, and returns only unapproved rows. Preserve a companion approved-results report and raw events.

Normalization is intentionally conservative. It does not resolve 8.3 paths, environment variables, symlinks, device paths, or quoted-argument semantics because those transformations can change identity. Microsoft states environment variables in SetNotifyCmdLine are not expanded; preserve raw values for response.

## Step 5 — CIM and outcome correlation

Keep `cimModels=[]`. Change.All_Changes has no guaranteed BITS job/command schema, and Endpoint.Processes records actual process creation rather than callback configuration. A deployment-owned summary may store the post-detection event only after parity tests and raw references.

Collect event 3 job creation, event 16403 file addition, transfer lifecycle events, current `Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers`/COM inventory, Security 4688 or Sysmon 1, PowerShell 4103/4104, EDR, file creation/hash/signature, DNS/network, and authentication evidence under separate contracts. Microsoft documents `Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers` requires administrative credentials; protect output and do not disrupt jobs during collection.

To prove callback execution, find a process whose image/arguments match the raw callback after the configured job reaches ERROR or TRANSFERRED, with appropriate user/session and BITS service ancestry/context. Account for Microsoft-documented nonexecution conditions. Temporal proximity alone is not sufficient, and absence of a process may reflect service ownership, valid COM callback, collection gap, or state not reached.

## Step 6 — Validate detection and nonclaims

Create fixed-time event-6 fixtures for XML and classic rendering, alias capitalization, mixed case, repeated whitespace, quoted paths, empty parameters, empty program removal, malformed job GUID, missing owner/record ID, wrong provider/channel/source/type, event 3, event 16403, duplicate routes, late events, and provider-version drift. Assert raw preservation, normalized command, SHA-256, one-row grain, and no URL/execution fields.

Test approval at exact inclusive start, one second before end, exactly at exclusive end, future/expired window, wrong host/owner/hash, one-character argument change, missing governance fields, malformed epoch, duplicate lookup key, stale bundle, and wildcard rejection. Exactly-at-end must alert. Compare independently computed hashes from test code and SPL.

For runtime validation, use a harmless signed callback on a disposable host. Test a normal user-owned job that reaches the selected notification state and separately test LocalSystem/NetworkService ownership to document the no-command-line-callback behavior Microsoft describes. Test a valid COM callback only with BITS engineering review. Never download or execute public malware, weaken controls, or register a production interpreter callback merely to generate telemetry.

Load-test updater bursts, long parameter strings, event truncation, WEC fan-in, duplicate routes, lookup bundles, hashing, scheduler overlap, RBAC, and retention. Ensure raw command data is access-controlled because arguments may contain URLs, tokens, usernames, or file paths.

## Step 7 — Alert, investigate, and respond

Alert title: `Unapproved BITS notification command configured on <host>`. Include UTC event/index time, host, job ID/owner, raw program/parameters, command hash, provider/channel/version/record ID, approval state/revision, source/schema health, software owner, and restricted raw link.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw event XML, provider/channel/version/template, record identity, extraction, normalization/hash, and duplicate route.
2. Re-evaluate exact approval, UTC boundaries, lookup checksum/revision, package/change ID, owner, and approver.
3. Enumerate the job by exact GUID without modifying it; record state/type/priority/owner/age, files/remote and local names, notification flags/interface/command, retry settings, and current availability.
4. Identify creating/configuring process through event 3, process start key/PID where available, PowerShell/BITSAdmin/COM telemetry, user/session, parent, signer/hash, and management job.
5. Determine whether callback could execute: job owner context, target state, notify flags, valid COM callback, and actual process evidence.
6. Inspect transfer destination/source, local file, hashes/signatures, network behavior, child processes, persistence, and adjacent endpoint alerts.
7. Validate software deployment, updater, security product, support, test, or exercise evidence against exact command.
8. If unauthorized, follow accountable endpoint/identity incident procedure to preserve BITS/database/process/file evidence, contain risk, and cancel/remove only with owner approval.
9. Revalidate job cleanup, software integrity, channel/schema health, and no recurrence before closure.

Do not automatically cancel or complete the job, delete downloaded files, kill a callback, quarantine software, isolate a host, or disable BITS from event 6 alone. Those actions can disrupt Windows Update, enterprise distribution, or business applications and can destroy evidence.

## Step 8 — Troubleshooting and maintenance

- **No event 6:** verify installed provider template/version, Operational channel enabled, actual SetNotifyCmdLine success, input/WEC subscription, forwarder queues, source/type/index/RBAC, and channel overwrite.
- **Fields null:** inspect provider Template and raw XML; fix add-on/extraction for the qualified build. Do not regex localized Message text without a versioned test contract.
- **Many updater callbacks:** onboard exact host/owner/full-command hashes through package governance; do not suppress signer/path families.
- **Hash mismatch:** compare raw case/whitespace/quotes, normalization order, delimiter, UTF-8/hash implementation, and lookup generation.
- **No callback process:** check job state, owner service context, notification flags/interface, Microsoft-documented precedence, process-source health, and timing before concluding prevention.
- **Job absent:** it may already be completed/cancelled/aged out; preserve event evidence and use retained inventory/forensics rather than claiming false telemetry.
- **Duplicate alerts:** compare host/source/record ID, WEC subscriptions, queue replay, overlap checkpoint, and search throttling; never throttle only by program.
- **CIM process mismatch:** expected; configuration and execution are different event grains.

Review host/build/provider inventory, template checksums, channel/source health, fields, delay window, command normalization/hash, approvals, BITS policies/inventory, callback outcome correlation, ATT&CK version, RBAC/retention, dashboard, alert, runbook, and exceptions quarterly and after Windows, provider, BITS, updater, endpoint-management, WEC/forwarder, add-on, lookup, or Splunk changes. Keep `status=draft` until Windows/BITS, software, and Splunk owners execute and sign the matrix.
grandmaExplanation: Windows can quietly download files in the background and can be told to run a program when a job finishes or fails. We flag any such run command that was not exactly approved, but we still check other logs before saying the program actually ran.
